title: Oxidation–reduction reactions
competency: Identify oxidation, reduction and the agents, find oxidation numbers, and balance redox equations by oxidation number and half-reaction methods.

keywords.def: Loss of electrons; the oxidation number increases.
Gain of electrons; the oxidation number decreases.
The species that is reduced: it takes electrons from another species.
The species that is oxidized: it gives electrons to another species.
The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. Elements are 0.
A reaction in which electrons move from one species to another, so oxidation and reduction happen together.
The oxidation part or the reduction part of a redox reaction, written with electrons.

en.text: Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number goes up); reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation number goes down). They always happen together in a redox reaction. The oxidizing agent is the species reduced; the reducing agent is the species oxidized. Oxidation numbers add up to 0 in a compound and to the charge in an ion.

am.text: ኦክሳይዴሽን ኤሌክትሮን ማጣት፣ ሪዳክሽን ኤሌክትሮን መቀበል ነው። ሁለቱም አብረው ይከሰታሉ። ኦክሳይድ አድራጊው ራሱ ይቀነሳል።

screens.title: Magnesium in acid
screens.ask: A magnesium ribbon fizzes in hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What happens to the Mg atoms?
opts: They lose electrons and become Mg²⁺
screens.after: Mg goes from 0 to +2: it loses two electrons (oxidation). H⁺ gains them and becomes H₂ (reduction).
screens.best: They lose electrons and become Mg²⁺

screens.title: Oxidation and reduction
paras: Oxidation: loss of electrons; the oxidation number increases.
Reduction: gain of electrons; the oxidation number decreases.
They always occur together, so we call them redox reactions.
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: Mg 0 → +2 (oxidized), H +1 → 0 (reduced). Cl⁻ is a spectator.

screens.title: Rules for oxidation numbers
screens.ask: Tap each card to see a rule and an example.
items: Every atom in an element is 0: Mg, O₂, Cl₂, S₈.
Usually −2, as in H₂O. In peroxides (H₂O₂) it is −1.
Usually +1, as in HCl. In metal hydrides (NaH) it is −1.
Group 1 is always +1 (Na, K). Group 2 is always +2 (Mg, Ca).
Equal to its charge: Cl⁻ is −1, Fe³⁺ is +3.
The total is 0 in a compound and the charge in an ion.

screens.title: Agents and oxidation numbers
paras: The oxidizing agent takes electrons, so it is reduced.
The reducing agent gives electrons, so it is oxidized.
Elements: 0. O: usually −2. H: usually +1. Group 1 metals: +1.
The numbers add to 0 in a compound and to the charge in an ion.

screens.title: Find Cr in K₂CrO₄, one step at a time
steps: Write what you know: K = +1, O = −2, Cr = x.
K₂CrO₄ is neutral, so the total is 0.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Loss of electrons; the oxidation number increases.
Gain of electrons; the oxidation number decreases.
The species that is reduced: it takes electrons from another species.
The species that is oxidized: it gives electrons to another species.
The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. Elements are 0.

screens.text: Identify the oxidizing agent in Mg(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Zn(s) + Mg²⁺(aq):
screens.why:
Step 1: Mg goes 0 → +2. It loses 2e⁻, so Mg is oxidized.
Step 2: Zn²⁺ goes +2 → 0. It gains 2e⁻, so Zn²⁺ is reduced.
Step 3: the species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.
So the oxidizing agent is Zn²⁺.
Trap: Mg is the reducing agent. Zn and Mg²⁺ are products, not agents.
screens.clue: The oxidizing agent is itself reduced.

screens.ask: Find the oxidation number of Cr in K₂CrO₄: +___
screens.why:
Step 1: K (Group 1) is +1; O is −2. Let Cr = x.
Step 2: a neutral compound adds to 0: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0.
Step 3: 2 + x − 8 = 0, so x = +6.
Check: +2 + 6 − 8 = 0. Cr is +6.

screens.ask: Find the oxidation number of Cl in perchloric acid, HClO₄: +___
screens.why:
Step 1: H is +1; each O is −2. Let Cl = x.
Step 2: the acid is neutral: +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0.
Step 3: 1 + x − 8 = 0, so x = +7.
Check: +1 + 7 − 8 = 0. Cl is +7, its highest state.

screens.ask: Find the oxidation number of C in the oxalate ion, C₂O₄²⁻: +___
screens.why:
Step 1: each O is −2. Let each C = x.
Step 2: an ion adds to its charge: 2x + 4(−2) = −2.
Step 3: 2x − 8 = −2, so 2x = 6 and x = +3.
Trap: do not set the sum to 0. This is an ion with charge −2.
screens.clue: The numbers add to the ion's charge, −2.

screens.title: Redox or not?
screens.why:
Step 1: a reaction is redox only if some oxidation numbers change.
Step 2: Ca + 2H₂O: Ca 0 → +2 and H +1 → 0. Redox.
Step 3: Mg + 2HCl: Mg 0 → +2 and H +1 → 0. Redox.
Step 4: H₂SO₄ + NaOH (neutralization) and AgNO₃ + NaCl (precipitation): ions only swap partners. No number changes, so not redox.
Tip: a free element on one side usually means redox.
screens.clue: Look for an element on one side and an ion on the other.
screens.ask: Sort the reactions: is each one a redox reaction or not?

screens.text: Decide what is oxidized and what is reduced in 2Hg²⁺ + N₂H₄ → 2Hg + N₂ + 4H⁺:
opts: Hg²⁺ is reduced; N₂H₄ is oxidized
Hg²⁺ is oxidized; N₂H₄ is reduced
screens.ans: Hg²⁺ is reduced; N₂H₄ is oxidized
screens.why:
Step 1: Hg goes +2 → 0. A fall means a gain of electrons: Hg²⁺ is reduced.
Step 2: N in N₂H₄: 2x + 4(+1) = 0, so x = −2.
Step 3: N goes −2 → 0 in N₂. A rise means a loss of electrons: N₂H₄ is oxidized.
So Hg²⁺ is reduced and N₂H₄ is oxidized.
Check: 2 Hg gain 4e⁻; 2 N lose 4e⁻.
screens.clue: Find the oxidation number of N in N₂H₄ first.

screens.text: Find the oxidation numbers of Ni, S and O in Ni₂(SO₄)₃:
screens.why:
Step 1: O is −2.
Step 2: in SO₄²⁻: x + 4(−2) = −2, so S = +6.
Step 3: three sulfates carry 3 × (−2) = −6.
Step 4: 2 Ni must give +6, so Ni = +3.
Answer: Ni +3, S +6, O −2.
Trap: Ni +2 would need NiSO₄, not Ni₂(SO₄)₃.

screens.ask: Find the oxidation number of N in hydrazine, N₂H₄: ___
screens.why:
Step 1: H with a non-metal is +1. Let each N = x.
Step 2: the molecule is neutral: 2x + 4(+1) = 0.
Step 3: 2x = −4, so x = −2.
Check: 2(−2) + 4 = 0. N is −2 (write the minus sign).

ideas.name: Balancing by change in oxidation number

en.text: To balance a redox equation by oxidation numbers: assign oxidation numbers, find which atoms change and by how many electrons, multiply so that electrons lost equal electrons gained, use the multipliers as coefficients, and finish the other atoms by inspection.

am.text: በኦክሳይዴሽን ቁጥር ለውጥ ማመጣጠን፡ የጠፉ ኤሌክትሮኖች ከተቀበሉት ጋር እኩል እንዲሆኑ አባዛ፣ ቀሪውን በምልከታ አመጣጥን።

screens.title: How many electrons?
screens.ask: PbS + O₂ → PbO + SO₂. Sulfur goes from −2 in PbS to +4 in SO₂. How many electrons does each S lose?
screens.after:
S goes from −2 to +4. That is a rise of 6.
Each S loses 6 electrons.
Trap: 4 is only the final number, not the change.

screens.title: Six steps
paras: 1. Write the unbalanced equation.
2. Assign oxidation numbers.
3. Find the atoms oxidized and reduced.
4. Count electrons lost and gained.
5. Multiply so electrons lost = electrons gained; use the factors as coefficients.
6. Balance the rest by inspection.

screens.title: Balance PbS + O₂ → PbO + SO₂
steps: Assign numbers: S is −2 in PbS and +4 in SO₂. O is 0 in O₂ and −2 in the products.
LCM of 6 and 4 is 12: 2 S lose 12e⁻; 3 O₂ gain 12e⁻.
Check O: 6 on the left; 2 + 4 = 6 on the right.

screens.title: Key word
defs: A reaction in which electrons move from one species to another, so oxidation and reduction happen together.

screens.text: Track nitrogen in Cu + HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO + H₂O. What does N do?
screens.why:
Step 1: N in HNO₃: +1 + x − 6 = 0, so x = +5.
Step 2: N in NO: x − 2 = 0, so x = +2.
Step 3: +5 → +2 is a fall of 3.
Step 4: a fall in oxidation number is a gain of electrons: 3e⁻ per N.
Trap: "loses 3e⁻" mixes up the direction. Down = gain = reduction.
screens.clue: Work out N in HNO₃ and in NO.

screens.ask: Balance by change in oxidation number: 2PbS + ___O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂
screens.why:
Step 1: S goes −2 → +4: each S loses 6e⁻. 2 S lose 12e⁻.
Step 2: O goes 0 → −2: each O₂ gains 2 × 2 = 4e⁻.
Step 3: electrons lost = gained: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 O₂.
Check O: left 3 × 2 = 6; right 2 (PbO) + 4 (SO₂) = 6. Answer: 3.

screens.ask: Balance by change in oxidation number: KClO₃ + ___HBr → 3Br₂ + 3H₂O + KCl
screens.why:
Step 1: Cl goes +5 (KClO₃) → −1 (KCl): one Cl gains 6e⁻.
Step 2: Br goes −1 (HBr) → 0 (Br₂): each Br loses 1e⁻.
Step 3: 6 Br must lose 6e⁻, so 6 HBr (that gives 3Br₂).
Check H: 6 H in 6HBr = 6 H in 3H₂O. O: 3 = 3. Answer: 6.

screens.text: Choose the correctly balanced equation for H₂S + HNO₃ → S + NO + H₂O:
screens.why:
Step 1: S goes −2 → 0: loses 2e⁻. N goes +5 → +2: gains 3e⁻.
Step 2: LCM of 2 and 3 is 6: 3 H₂S and 2 HNO₃.
Step 3: H on the left: 3 × 2 + 2 = 8, so 4H₂O.
Step 4: check O: left 2 × 3 = 6; right 2 + 4 = 6.
Answer: 3H₂S + 2HNO₃ → 3S + 2NO + 4H₂O.
Trap: the option with 2H₂O balances electrons but not H and O.

screens.ask: Balance copper with concentrated nitric acid: Cu + ___HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O
screens.why:
Step 1: Cu goes 0 → +2: loses 2e⁻.
Step 2: N goes +5 (HNO₃) → +4 (NO₂): gains 1e⁻ each. So 2 NO₂.
Step 3: Cu(NO₃)₂ needs 2 more NO₃⁻ that are not reduced.
Step 4: HNO₃ = 2 (reduced) + 2 (salt) = 4.
Check H: 4 = 2 × 2 in 2H₂O. O: 12 = 6 + 4 + 2. Answer: 4.
screens.clue: Some HNO₃ is reduced, some just forms the salt.

screens.title: The six steps in order
screens.text: Put the steps for balancing by oxidation number in order.
items: Find the atoms oxidized and reduced
Multiply so electrons lost = electrons gained
screens.why:
Step 1: you need an equation before you can assign numbers.
Step 2: the numbers show which atoms change.
Step 3: the changes give the electrons lost and gained.
Step 4: multipliers make lost = gained.
Step 5: atoms that do not change (H, O, spectators) go last, by inspection.
screens.clue: You cannot count electrons until you have oxidation numbers.

screens.why:
Step 1: the electrons already match (N gains 3e⁻ × 2; As loses 2e⁻ × 3).
Step 2: count H on the left: 2 + 3 × 3 = 11.
Step 3: H on the right in 3H₃AsO₄: 9. 11 − 9 = 2 H, so 1 H₂O.
Check O: left 6 + 9 = 15; right 2 + 12 + 1 = 15. Answer: 1.

en.text: Split the reaction into an oxidation half and a reduction half. Balance atoms other than O and H, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with electrons. Multiply so the electrons cancel and add the halves. In basic solution, finish as if acidic, then add OH⁻ equal to the H⁺ to both sides and turn H⁺ + OH⁻ into H₂O.

am.text: በግማሽ ግብረመልስ ዘዴ፡ O በH₂O፣ H በH⁺፣ ቻርጅ በኤሌክትሮን አመጣጥን፤ ኤሌክትሮኖቹ እንዲሰረዙ አባዛ።

screens.title: Where do the electrons go?
screens.ask: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺. To balance the charge, where do we write the electron?
opts: On the right, as a product
On the left, as a reactant
screens.after: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. In oxidation the electrons are products; in reduction they are reactants.
screens.best: On the right, as a product

screens.title: Half-reaction steps (acidic)
paras: 1. Split into oxidation and reduction halves.
2. Balance atoms other than O and H.
3. Balance O with H₂O, then H with H⁺.
4. Balance charge with e⁻.
5. Multiply so electrons are equal; add; check atoms and charge.
Basic solution: add OH⁻ equal to H⁺ to both sides; H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; cancel water.

screens.title: Dichromate and iron(II)
steps: Reduction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O; add 14H⁺; charge +12 vs +6, so add 6e⁻.
Multiply the iron half by 6 and add: 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ + Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 6Fe³⁺ + 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.

screens.title: In basic solution: MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ → MnO₂ + I₂
steps: Basic: add 8OH⁻ to both sides. 8H⁺ + 8OH⁻ become 8H₂O.
Check charge: −8 on each side. O: 12 = 12. H: 8 = 8.

screens.title: Key word
defs: The oxidation part or the reduction part of a redox reaction, written with electrons.

screens.text: Choose the balanced reduction half-reaction for MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ in acid:
screens.why:
Step 1: Mn is already balanced (1 = 1).
Step 2: balance O with water: 4 O → 4H₂O on the right.
Step 3: balance H with H⁺: 8H⁺ on the left.
Step 4: charge: left −1 + 8 = +7; right +2. Add 5e⁻ to the left.
Answer: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
Trap: electrons on the right would make it an oxidation.
screens.clue: Balance O, then H, then charge.

screens.why:
Step 1: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O takes 6e⁻.
Step 2: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ gives 1e⁻ each.
Step 3: 6 Fe²⁺ give the 6e⁻.
Check charge: left −2 + 12 + 14 = +24; right 6 + 18 = +24. Answer: 6.

Step 1: reduction × 2: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10e⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O.
Step 2: oxidation × 5: 5H₂C₂O₄ → 10CO₂ + 10H⁺ + 10e⁻.
Step 3: add; 10H⁺ cancel from 16H⁺, so 6H⁺ remain on the left.
Check charge: left −2 + 6 = +4; right 2 × (+2) = +4. Answer: 6.

screens.text: How do you finish a half-reaction balance in basic solution?
opts: add OH⁻ equal to the H⁺ to both sides
remove all H⁺ from one side
screens.ans: add OH⁻ equal to the H⁺ to both sides
screens.why:
Step 1: balance first as if the solution were acidic (with H⁺).
Step 2: add as many OH⁻ as there are H⁺, to BOTH sides.
Step 3: each H⁺ + OH⁻ on one side becomes H₂O.
Step 4: cancel water that appears on both sides.
Trap: adding OH⁻ to one side only breaks the balance.

screens.title: Half-reaction steps in order
screens.text: Put the steps of the half-reaction method (acidic solution) in order.
items: Split into oxidation and reduction halves
Balance atoms other than O and H
Multiply so electrons are equal, then add
screens.why:
Step 1: split the reaction into two halves.
Step 2: balance the main atoms first (Cr, Mn, Fe …).
Step 3: O comes from water, so add H₂O next.
Step 4: the water brings H, so then add H⁺.
Step 5: only now is the charge fixed with e⁻.
Step 6: equal electrons cancel when the halves are added.
screens.clue: Electrons are added only after all atoms balance.

screens.text: Balance in basic solution: Pb(OH)₄²⁻ + ClO⁻ → PbO₂ + Cl⁻ + OH⁻ + H₂O. How many OH⁻ and electrons?
screens.why:
Step 1: Pb +2 → +4 loses 2e⁻; Cl +1 → −1 gains 2e⁻. So 2 electrons move.
Step 2: one of each reactant is enough: Pb(OH)₄²⁻ + ClO⁻ → PbO₂ + Cl⁻ + ?OH⁻ + ?H₂O.
Step 3: charge: left −3. Right −1 − x = −3, so 2 OH⁻.
Step 4: H: 4 = 2 (OH⁻) + 2 (H₂O). O: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1.
Answer: 2 OH⁻ and 2 electrons.
screens.clue: Find the change in oxidation numbers first.

screens.why:
Step 1: BrO₃⁻ → Br⁻: 3 O become 3H₂O.
Step 2: 3H₂O hold 6 H, so 6H⁺ on the left.
Step 3: Br +5 → −1 takes 6e⁻; 6Fe²⁺ give 6e⁻.
Check charge: left −1 + 12 + 6 = +17; right −1 + 18 = +17. Answer: 6.

test.ask: Find the oxidation number of S in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻: +___
test.why:
Step 1: O is −2. Let S = x.
Step 2: an ion adds to its charge: x + 4(−2) = −2.
Step 3: x − 8 = −2, so x = +6.
Trap: setting the sum to 0 gives +8, which is wrong.

test.text: Define a reducing agent. It is the substance that is
test.why:
Step 1: a reducing agent gives electrons to another species.
Step 2: losing electrons is oxidation.
So the reducing agent is itself oxidized.
Trap: "reduced" describes the oxidizing agent.

test.text: Name the role of Cl₂ in 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl:
test.why:
Step 1: Na goes 0 → +1: Na is oxidized.
Step 2: Cl goes 0 → −1: Cl₂ gains electrons, so it is reduced.
Step 3: the species reduced is the oxidizing agent.
So Cl₂ is the oxidizing agent; Na is the reducing agent.

test.ask: Count the electrons: in MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺, each Mn gains ___ electrons
test.why:
Step 1: Mn in MnO₄⁻: x − 8 = −1, so x = +7.
Step 2: Mn in Mn²⁺ is +2.
Step 3: +7 → +2 is a fall of 5, so 5 electrons are gained.
Answer: 5.

test.ask: Balance copper with hot concentrated sulfuric acid: Cu + SO₄²⁻ + ___H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + SO₂ + 2H₂O
test.why:
Step 1: Cu 0 → +2 loses 2e⁻; S +6 → +4 gains 2e⁻. Electrons match 1 : 1.
Step 2: O: SO₄²⁻ has 4 O; SO₂ keeps 2, so 2 O go to 2H₂O.
Step 3: 2H₂O hold 4 H, so 4H⁺.
Check charge: left −2 + 4 = +2; right +2. Answer: 4.

Example 2.2 Q2 calls manganese(IV) oxide "MnO₄⁻"; it is MnO₂.
